_comment: Hand corrections over the reader's output for A4, in integer pixels of
x,y is the box CENTRE, not its top-left corner.
The reader found 25 of the board's 71 designators. That is 35% on paper and
much better than it sounds: 35 of the 71 are rivets, spacers, screws, cable
ties, feet, the fuse holder and two cables, none of which has a silkscreen
designator at all, and they are listed under notOnDrawing below. Of the 36
parts that are actually printed on the drawing the reader placed 24
correctly, misplaced one (F1) and missed eleven; all twelve are placed by
hand here off scripts/page_grid.py at 1:1 over .build/a4/drawing_full.png.
Every one of the reader's 25 was rendered and looked at, agreed tier
included. Nineteen agreed, five were single and one was ambiguous; the
nineteen and the five were all right, and the ambiguous one was F1, which
the reader had put on a dashed hidden outline in the middle of the board
about 2000 px from the real fuse holder.
_layersComment: Registration of the photograph against the locator drawing, from which
build_coords.py solves the board -> photo homography. 'src' is board space
(the drawing), 'dst' is photo space; both are normalised, not pixels.
This board is registered from its outline rather than from its silkscreen.
It is a lazy L -- a long section spanning the full width with a vertical
arm at the right-hand end -- photographed as a dark blue board on white
paper, so the edge is the highest-contrast thing in either image, while the
silkscreen that A20 was matched on is here down to the assembly legend, the
three high-voltage warnings and the two jumper tables, several of them under
the looms. The board outline was
extracted from both images and the whole contour matched, not a few of its
corners: the bottom edge over its full 2.4 kpx run, the top edge of the
long section, the left edge, the right edge, the arm's top edge and both
sections of the arm's left edge -- 5309 outline pixels of the drawing, laid
on the seven edges the photograph shows unobstructed.
Each of those pixels is required to land on the *line* of its photographed
edge, not on any particular point of it. That is the whole trick: a point
in the middle of a long straight edge is a real measurement across the edge
and no measurement at all along it, and a fit that pretends otherwise is
the one that goes wrong. Matching the contours point to point instead --
closest-point ICP -- pulls on the corners, which the drawing draws sharp
and the photograph shows rounded, and comes out 20 px off along the right
edge and 47 px off at the bottom-right corner. The line fit holds every
one of the seven edges to a mean of 6.4 px or better and 10.5 px at worst.
What was masked out, and why. The mains and rear-panel looms cross the
outline in three places on the photograph -- the black bundle looping off
the right-hand edge of the arm (and back over that edge around y 0.5-0.7),
the same bundle and its tie-wrap lying over the inner corner of the L, and
the line-filter bracket standing over the bottom-left corner -- and F1 and
SW2-SW4 stand out over the right edge below the arm. Those five stretches
are excluded on the photograph and the matching stretches are excluded on
the drawing, so that neither side pulls on the other. On the drawing the
mains lead and its plug, which are drawn outside the board outline, are
excluded too. Nothing here is on a mounting hole or a standoff, and this
assembly has no ejector levers at all.
The landmarks below are that fit expressed as pairs: points sampled along
every one of the seven edges, spaced from the left edge beside J21 to the
top of the arm above P82, plus the three corners that two measured edges
actually reach. A pair on an edge is checkable across the edge -- open both
images there and both points sit on the board edge beside the part named --
and it follows the fit along it, because nothing in either image says where
along a straight edge a point is. The three corner pairs are the only ones
pinned in both directions.
How good it is, measured rather than asserted. Against the 5309 outline
pixels the shipped homography lands a median 1.4 px, p90 5.1 px and worst
10.5 px off the photographed edge, in pixels of the 3400 px photo the
browser loads. The homography these 26 landmarks solve to agrees with the
fit made directly to all 5309 pixels to within 3.0 px everywhere on the
board, median 0.6 px -- i.e. the landmarks reproduce the whole-contour fit
rather than re-anchoring it somewhere. The residual that is left is
systematic, not noise: the arm comes out about 10 px wider on the
photograph than the drawing scales to, which no single projective transform
removes.
One region is spanned rather than anchored: the bottom-right corner, where
F1, SW2-SW4 and the loom hide the board edge in the photograph. Nothing
pins that corner directly; it is carried by the bottom edge and the arm's
right edge, which both run past it. The markers there were checked by eye
and land, but that is the one part of the board where the fit is an
extension of two measurements rather than a measurement.
Checked the way that actually catches a bad fit. All 36 reviewed board
positions -- this board has only 36, and 35 further parts with no
silkscreen designator at all, so the population is a third of A20's 112 --
were drawn onto the photograph through this homography and looked at in
tiles from J21 at the far left to SW2 at the far right, and the whole
drawing was warped over the photograph so that the printed part outlines
could be compared with the parts themselves. Every marker lands on its own
part. In particular J13, J16 and J41, which the rejected five-corner fit
put about 180 px right of theirs, now land on their connectors, and F1, SW2
and J91, which that fit did get right, still do.
For the record, what was rejected before this: a fit to five outline
corners, read off a pixel grid by eye. It solved cleanly -- worst residual
6 px of 3400 -- and was wrong by 180 px across the middle of the board,
because three of the five corners of an L sit in its right-hand quarter, so
the fit was anchored there and spanned everywhere else. A 6 px residual on
five clustered points says nothing about the rest of the board; the sweep
above is what says it.

_boardComment: Twelve hand placements. Each box is the silkscreen designator text, read off
a 1:1 pixel grid over .build/a4/drawing_full.png, so it is the same kind of
geometry the reader produces for the other twenty-four.

F1.note: Silkscreen F1 inside the fuse holder outline at the top right, above RV2 and SW4. Replaces the reader's ambiguous marker, which was on a hidden outline near J41.

RV2.note: Vertical silkscreen inside the varistor's oval body outline, between F1 and the SW3/SW4 pair. The label reads bottom-to-top, so the box is tall and narrow.

J16.note: Inside the J16 header outline, above R2.

R2.note: Inside the R2 body outline, between J16 and CR4. The fan 1 current sense resistor.

CR4.note: Below its diode symbol, above C1.

C1.note: Above the capacitor's arc outline, below CR4 and above J51.

J51.note: Inside the J51 header outline. Fan 1 connector.

R1.note: Right of the resistor's vertical body outline, right of J73.

C6.note: Left of RV1, above C4. The guard snubber capacitor.

R4.note: Right of RV1, below its horizontal body outline.

J52.note: Inside the J52 header outline, left of J11. Fan 2 connector.

J91.note: Inside the J91 ribbon header outline at the bottom edge, right of J62.

_schematicComment: Sheet corrections. All 68 markers the reader placed across the three sheets
were rendered and looked at, agreed tier included, and the three sheets came
out very differently:
sh1  3 of 18 kept.  The worst of the three, and for a reason that is
visible at a glance: sheet 1 carries perhaps eight real designators
and one large table of nothing but numbers. Twelve of the fifteen
wrong markers are on that table (SW2/SW3/SW4 on its own column
headers, J15 on the row '115', R1 on 'RIGHT=0'), on a caption
('MOTHERBOARD', 'SWITCH'), or on a part that is explicitly NOT on
this board (F1 landed on FL1, the line filter; P81 on P31, the line
cord connector).
sh2  6 of 22 kept.  Sheet 2 is one large interconnect and the reader read
the transformer's winding labels as designators: J13 onto 'S2 -13',
SW2 onto 'S2 -12', SW3 onto 'S3 -2', SW4 onto 'S4 -3'. The rest
landed on pin numbers and net names ('PA LAC1' as C1, '5 FR1 AC2' as
sh3  20 of 28 kept.  The best sheet in the assembly by a wide margin,
because its designators are isolated labels beside real symbols
rather than text inside tables. Eighteen of its twenty agreed
markers were right. The two that were not are the same trap twice:
P81 and P82 landed on P51 and P52, the fan plugs, which are marked
NOT ON MOTHERBOARD.
Seven markers are hand-placed: F1 and SW2-SW4 on sheet 1, where the reader
had all four on the switch configuration table or on the line filter, and
R4, C6 and P82 on sheet 2. Everything else the sheets needed was either
already right or is genuinely not drawn on that sheet.

F1.note: Beside the fuse symbol in the MAIN FUSE HOLDER block, above the '3.0A SLO' annotation. The reader had F1 on FL1, the ac line filter, which is inside the HARDWARE NOT ON THE MOTHERBOARD box.

SW2.note: Under the 2P2TSW symbol carrying pins L1/R3/L4/R6 — the switch itself. The reader had it on the SW2 column header of the switch configuration table, which is the relay-state-table trap in a different costume.

SW3.note: SW3's upper 2P2TSW block, the one fed from pin 2. It is drawn twice on this sheet, once per pole; the lower block sits at about (3765, 1971). The reader had SW3 on the table's column header.

SW4.note: SW4's upper 2P2TSW block. As with SW3 it is drawn twice, the second at about (4075, 2154). The reader had SW4 on the table's column header.

R4.note: Beside the resistor symbol in the guard snubber, above its '68' value. The reader never found it.

C6.note: Beside the capacitor symbol below R4, above its '6800pf' value. The reader had read this label as C5, which is on sheet 3.

P82.note: Inside the P82 connector block. The reader's box had the right centre but was 248 px wide, three times the label; tightened rather than moved.
